title: Demersal fish in three Alaska trawl surveys experienced about 93% of year-to-year bottom temperature anomalies in 1982-2026; a thermal-niche model predicted about 55%
abstract: Question: when the sea floor is warmer or colder than usual, do demersal fish move to keep their usual temperature, or do they experience the full anomaly? Data: three NOAA AFSC bottom trawl surveys with haul bottom temperatures and area-swept catches: eastern Bering Sea shelf (44 surveys, 1982-2026), Gulf of Alaska (15 surveys, 1993-2025) and Aleutian Islands (14 surveys, 1994-2026); 98 demersal fish taxa and 48 low-mobility invertebrate taxa as a negative control. Method: for each taxon and year we compared the observed catch-weighted bottom temperature with the temperature that the taxon would experience on its usual map (mean distribution of the other years). We used fixed-footprint cells with design weights and a correction for year-to-year station placement. The exposure slope is 1 for no buffering by redistribution and 0 for full buffering. Results: fish slopes were 0.90 (95% year-bootstrap CI 0.86-0.94) in the Bering Sea, 0.98 (0.95-1.03) in the Gulf of Alaska and 0.92 (0.87-0.99) in the Aleutians; combined 0.94 (0.91-0.96). A Gaussian thermal-niche (space-for-time) model predicted 0.55 (0.51-0.59). The fish realised 23%, 4% and 20% of the predicted buffering. Taxa with a stronger predicted response buffered more, but only 0.2-0.4 times as much as predicted. Buffering did not fail in the warmest years (2014-2021 heatwaves), and we found no consistent movement to deeper water. Results were stable for other cell sizes, survey strata, raw temperatures, biomass and survey-day controls, and time periods. Invertebrate controls gave 0.98 and 1.03 in the Bering Sea and Aleutians, but 0.80 in the Gulf of Alaska (0.90 from 2000), so the Gulf of Alaska contrast is not interpretable. Limitations: movement out of the survey footprint is not seen; temperature-dependent catchability can affect the weights; the niche model is a simple benchmark; all surveys are in Alaska.

citations.reason: We reuse its archived AFSC haul, EBS catch and species files and its FOSS retrieval code. We extend its EBS study to experienced temperature in three regions.
It found that bird community temperature indices tracked less than 10% of warming. We find a similar small tracking of interannual bottom temperature by demersal fish.
Fish community responses to warming depend on thermal affinities and depth-temperature gradients.
Marine heatwaves were not a dominant driver of demersal fish change; our fish experienced heatwave anomalies but did not redistribute much.
